Our results suggest that the primary cost of agentic software engineering lies not in initial code generation but in automated refinement and verification. Our novel methodology can help practitioners predict expenses and optimize workflows, and it directs future research toward developing more token-efficient agent collaboration protocols.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Will Blatantly Lie About Their Reasoning
papers.abstract: It has been shown that Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) may not *say what they think*: they do not always volunteer information about how certain parts of the input influence their reasoning. But it is one thing for a model to *omit* such information and another, worse thing to *lie* about it. Here, we extend the work of Chen et al. (2025) to show that LRMs will do just this: they will flatly deny relying on hints provided in the prompt in answering multiple choice questions -- even when directly asked to reflect on unusual (i.e. hinted) prompt content, even when allowed to use hints, and even though experiments *show* them to be using the hints. Our results thus have discouraging implications for CoT monitoring and interpretability.

papers.title: Just Enough Thinking: Efficient Reasoning with Adaptive Length Penalties Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve higher performance on challenging reasoning tasks by generating more tokens at inference time, but this verbosity often wastes computation on easy problems. Existing solutions, including supervised finetuning on shorter traces, user-controlled budgets, or RL with uniform penalties, either require data curation, manual configuration, or treat all problems alike regardless of difficulty. We introduce Adaptive Length Penalty (ALP), a reinforcement learning objective tailoring generation length to per-prompt solve rate. During training, ALP monitors each prompt's online solve rate through multiple rollouts and adds a differentiable penalty whose magnitude scales inversely with that rate, so confident (easy) prompts incur a high cost for extra tokens while hard prompts remain unhindered. Posttraining DeepScaleR-1.5B with ALP cuts average token usage by 50\% without significantly dropping performance. Relative to fixed-budget and uniform penalty baselines, ALP redistributes its reduced budget more intelligently by cutting compute on easy prompts and reallocating saved tokens to difficult ones, delivering higher accuracy on the hardest problems with higher cost.

papers.title: Multi-level models of language comprehension in the mind and brain
papers.abstract: What are the mental and neural representations that drive language understanding and acquisition? This thesis presents a two-part suite of methods for addressing these questions, rooted in the idea that representational claims must jointly assert a content — what a mental representation is about — but also a computational role — why it is there, and what concrete function it serves in bringing about language behavior. The first part of the thesis explores the computational role of syntactic and semantic representations in language acquisition and use. I instantiate a theory of syntactic bootstrapping, demonstrating through computational simulations how correspondences between the syntactic behaviors of words and their meanings can be exploited to efficiently construct a lexicon. This modeling work recapitulates classical dynamics of language learning exhibited by children acquiring their first language, and more broadly presents an expanded view of the computational role of these representational systems. The second part of the thesis addresses the neural side of these questions. I take a critical view on the present model-based cognitive neuroscience of language, arguing that some popular evaluation paradigms are limited in the types of claims about representational content they can safely support. I then present two case studies of a path forward, both exploiting measures drawn from modern large language models (LLMs). The first designs controlled interventions on LLMs’ internal representational contents, and tests the consequences of these interventions in a brain mapping evaluation. We apply this method in an fMRI brain decoding study, which reveals findings about the time-course of human syntactic representations. The second study integrates an LLM into a structured model of auditory word recognition, which is designed from the start for model interpretability. I apply this model to explain EEG data recorded as subjects listened to naturalistic English speech. The model enables us to discover distinct neural traces of how humans recognize and integrate the meanings of words in real time. I conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the mental computations that drive online language comprehension.

papers.title: Prioritizing Image-Related Tokens Enhances Vision-Language Pre-Training
papers.abstract: In standard large vision-language models (LVLMs) pre-training, the model typically maximizes the joint probability of the caption conditioned on the image via next-token prediction (NTP); however, since only a small subset of caption tokens directly relates to the visual content, this naive NTP unintentionally fits the model to noise and increases the risk of hallucination. We present PRIOR, a simple vision-language pre-training approach that addresses this issue by prioritizing image-related tokens through differential weighting in the NTP loss, drawing from the importance sampling framework. PRIOR introduces a reference model-a text-only large language model (LLM) trained on the captions without image inputs, to weight each token based on its probability for LVLMs training. Intuitively, tokens that are directly related to the visual inputs are harder to predict without the image and thus receive lower probabilities from the text-only reference LLM. During training, we implement a token-specific re-weighting term based on the importance scores to adjust each token's loss. We implement PRIOR in two distinct settings: LVLMs with visual encoders and LVLMs without visual encoders. We observe 19% and 8% average relative improvement, respectively, on several vision-language benchmarks compared to NTP. In addition, PRIOR exhibits superior scaling properties, as demonstrated by significantly higher scaling coefficients, indicating greater potential for performance gains compared to NTP given increasing compute and data.

papers.title: What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts
papers.abstract: Prompt underspecification is a common challenge when interacting with LLMs. In this paper, we present an in-depth analysis of this problem, showing that while LLMs can often infer unspecified requirements by default (41.1%), such behavior is fragile: Under-specified prompts are 2x as likely to regress across model or prompt changes, sometimes with accuracy drops exceeding 20%. This instability makes it difficult to reliably build LLM applications. Moreover, simply specifying all requirements does not consistently help, as models have limited instruction-following ability and requirements can conflict. Standard prompt optimizers likewise provide little benefit. To address these issues, we propose requirements-aware prompt optimization mechanisms that improve performance by 4.8% on average over baselines. We further advocate for a systematic process of proactive requirements discovery, evaluation, and monitoring to better manage prompt underspecification in practice.

papers.title: UTF:Undertrained Tokens as Fingerprints A Novel Approach to LLM Identification
papers.abstract: Fingerprinting large language models (LLMs) is essential for verifying model ownership, ensuring authenticity, and preventing misuse. Traditional fingerprinting methods often require significant computational overhead or white-box verification access. In this paper, we introduce UTF, a novel and efficient approach to fingerprinting LLMs by leveraging under-trained tokens. Under-trained tokens are tokens that the model has not fully learned during its training phase. By utilizing these tokens, we perform supervised fine-tuning to embed specific input-output pairs into the model. This process allows the LLM to produce predetermined outputs when presented with certain inputs, effectively embedding a unique fingerprint. Our method has minimal overhead and impact on model's performance, and does not require white-box access to target model's ownership identification. Compared to existing fingerprinting methods, UTF is also more effective and robust to fine-tuning and random guess.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Expanding Computation Spaces of LLMs at Inference Time
papers.research_question: Whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference time as expanded computation spaces, and how token types, numbers, insertion locations, training stage, and attention dynamics affect this.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can exploit filler tokens inserted at inference as expanded computation spaces to improve performance on QA and math tasks, with smaller models benefiting more, and attention analysis shows these spaces engage in meaningful computation.
papers.conclusion: Inserting filler tokens at inference provides expanded computation spaces that improve model performance, especially for smaller models, and these spaces are used meaningfully for answer inference as shown by attention analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models (e.g., 1.7B) benefit most from inserted filler tokens, with gains up to 12.372 percentage points, suggesting the spaces compensate for limited parameter capacity.
Optimal token types and counts vary across models; placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective.
Models progressively learn to leverage these spaces during pretraining and instruction-tuning, as shown by checkpoint analysis.
Attention map analysis reveals filler tokens attend to questions and answer options, influencing answer selection, rather than being redundant.
Performance degrades sharply when too many tokens (e.g., >1024) are added, resembling the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades when too many filler tokens are added, as models are not trained on such inputs.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) rationale enables language models to use additional task-related text for problem-solving, benefiting not only from detailed reasoning steps but also from the expanded computational space of longer inputs. Prior work has trained filler or special tokens to serve as additional computation spaces. In this study, we investigate whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference. We first identify effective token types, numbers, and insertion locations, then examine at what stage of training models begin to exploit the expanded computation space, and finally analyze dynamics within these spaces via attention maps. Experiments on models ranging from 1.7B to 32B across open-domain QA and math tasks show that appropriate token types and counts vary, but placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective. Smaller models benefit most, up to 12.372 percentage points in SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, indicating that these spaces act as additional computational capacity rather than redundant input. Attention maps reveal that expanded spaces often continue the original attention mechanism and sometimes focus on questions or answer options, suggesting meaningful computation for problem-solving.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
papers.research_question: What mechanisms cause extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in transformer-based LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the active-dormant mechanism and mutual reinforcement mechanism as the causes of extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in LLMs, and proposes architectural and optimization modifications to mitigate them.
papers.conclusion: The work uncovers the underlying mechanisms of extreme-token phenomena and suggests potential pathways to mitigate these issues during LLM pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extreme-token phenomena arise from an active-dormant mechanism in attention heads, where heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others.
A mutual reinforcement mechanism between attention sinks and value-state drains drives these phenomena during training.
In pretrained LLMs, many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the simplified Bigram-Backcopy task.
The quantitative properties of extreme-token dynamics in the Bigram-Backcopy task align with observations in pretrained LLMs, including sink-logits concentration.
Replacing softmax with ReLU in attention heads or Adam with SGD can mitigate extreme-token phenomena in the Bigram-Backcopy task.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena significantly improves downstream tasks like inference and quantization.
future_direction: Explore whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena is essential or beneficial for building powerful transformer-based LLMs.
Pretrain a model at the scale of GPT-2 to study the impact of mitigating extreme-token phenomena.
papers.abstract: Practitioners have consistently observed three puzzling phenomena in transformer-based large language models (LLMs): attention sinks, value-state drains, and residual-state peaks, collectively referred to as extreme-token phenomena. These phenomena are characterized by certain so-called "sink tokens" receiving disproportionately high attention weights, exhibiting significantly smaller value states, and having much larger residual-state norms than those of other tokens. These extreme tokens give rise to various challenges in LLM inference, quantization, and interpretability. We elucidate the mechanisms behind extreme-token phenomena. First, we show that these phenomena arise in very simple architectures -- transformers with one to three layers -- trained on a toy model, the Bigram-Backcopy (BB) task. In this setting, we identify an active-dormant mechanism, where attention heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others. Our theoretical analysis of the training dynamics reveals that these phenomena are driven by a mutual reinforcement mechanism. Building on these insights, we propose strategies to mitigate extreme-token phenomena during pretraining, including replacing softmax with ReLU and Adam with SGD. Next, we extend our analysis to pretrained LLMs, including Llama and OLMo, showing that many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the BB task, and that the mutual reinforcement mechanism also governs the emergence of extreme-token phenomena during LLM pretraining. Our results reveal that many of the static and dynamic properties of extreme-token phenomena predicted by the BB task align with observations in pretrained LLMs.

papers.title: LLM-Microscope: Uncovering the Hidden Role of Punctuation in Context Memory of Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) encode and store contextual information, and what is the role of seemingly minor tokens like punctuation and stopwords in this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LLM-Microscope, a toolkit for analyzing LLM internal representations, and reveals that 'filler' tokens like punctuation and stopwords are highly contextualized and critical for model performance on knowledge and reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Seemingly trivial 'filler' tokens play a critical role in maintaining context in LLMs, and their removal harms performance, highlighting the need for refined interpretability approaches; the LLM-Microscope toolkit facilitates such analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Tokens typically considered minor (determiners, punctuation, stopwords) carry surprisingly high contextual information and are key aggregators for language understanding.
Removing these 'filler' tokens consistently degrades performance on MMLU and BABILong-4k, even when removal is guided by a strong language model (GPT-4o).
A strong correlation exists between a token's contextualization level and the linearity of its transformation across model layers.
Intermediate layer representations predominantly correspond to English tokens even when processing non-English input, suggesting an implicit translation process.
The introduced LLM-Microscope toolkit provides methods for token-level nonlinearity analysis, contextual memory assessment, Logit Lens visualization, and intrinsic dimensionality measurement.
papers.limitation:
Using a pre-trained LM-head on intermediate embeddings without fine-tuning may not accurately reflect the actual functionality of these layers.
The accuracy of the adapter-based contextual memory assessment method may be influenced by the adapter's architecture, training data, and optimization process.
The results may not be equally applicable to all model architectures, sizes, or training paradigms.
papers.abstract: We introduce methods to quantify how Large Language Models (LLMs) encode and store contextual information, revealing that tokens often seen as minor (e.g., determiners, punctuation) carry surprisingly high context. Notably, removing these tokens -- especially stopwords, articles, and commas -- consistently degrades performance on MMLU and BABILong-4k, even if removing only irrelevant tokens. Our analysis also shows a strong correlation between contextualization and linearity, where linearity measures how closely the transformation from one layer's embeddings to the next can be approximated by a single linear mapping. These findings underscore the hidden importance of filler tokens in maintaining context. For further exploration, we present LLM-Microscope, an open-source toolkit that assesses token-level nonlinearity, evaluates contextual memory, visualizes intermediate layer contributions (via an adapted Logit Lens), and measures the intrinsic dimensionality of representations. This toolkit illuminates how seemingly trivial tokens can be critical for long-range understanding.

papers.title: Don't Take Things Out of Context: Attention Intervention for Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism by which isolated tokens in few-shot Chain-of-Thought demonstrations disrupt reasoning in LLMs, and how can we intervene to suppress this effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Few-shot Attention Intervention (FAI), a method that dynamically analyzes attention patterns to identify and suppress the distracting effect of isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations, thereby enhancing reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: FAI effectively recalibrates attention allocation to prevent LLMs from fixating on isolated tokens, enhancing reasoning performance across benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations can disrupt reasoning by causing the model to take information out of context.
Tokens with specific attention characteristics (high self-attention, direct influence on output) are responsible for this distracting effect.
FAI effectively identifies such tokens and improves performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
FAI improves accuracy on AQuA by 5.91% and on other datasets.
The distracting effect is estimated to cause about 60% of errors in certain cases.
papers.limitation: Experiments are confined to LLMs with parameter scale between 7 billion and 13 billion due to hardware constraints.
future_direction: Investigating larger models to gain further insights.
papers.abstract: Few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), functioning as a whole to guide these models in generating reasoning steps toward final answers. However, we observe that isolated segments, words, or tokens within CoT demonstrations can unexpectedly disrupt the generation process of LLMs. The model may overly concentrate on certain local information present in the demonstration, introducing irrelevant noise into the reasoning process and potentially leading to incorrect answers. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of CoT through dynamically tracing and manipulating the inner workings of LLMs at each output step, which demonstrates that tokens exhibiting specific attention characteristics are more likely to induce the model to take things out of context; these tokens directly attend to the hidden states tied with prediction, without substantial integration of non-local information. Building upon these insights, we propose a Few-shot Attention Intervention method (FAI) that dynamically analyzes the attention patterns of demonstrations to accurately identify these tokens and subsequently make targeted adjustments to the attention weights to effectively suppress their distracting effect on LLMs. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods, with a remarkable 5.91% improvement on the AQuA dataset, further highlighting the effectiveness of FAI.

papers.title: State over Tokens: Characterizing the Role of Reasoning Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of reasoning tokens in LLMs, given that they are not faithful explanations of the model's reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework, which reframes reasoning tokens as an externalized computational state that enables persistence across stateless generation cycles, explaining how they can drive correct reasoning without being faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens are best understood as an externalized computational state (SoT), which resolves misconceptions about their completeness and shared meaning, and opens new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations of the model's internal reasoning process.
Reasoning tokens function as an externalized computational state (SoT), the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles.
The SoT view explains two common misconceptions: the misconception of completeness (tokens externalize only what is necessary for the next cycle) and the misconception of shared meaning (tokens may use model-specific encodings not interpretable by humans).
The tokens inhabit distinct ontological categories: as natural language text for human readers and as a computational substrate for the model.
The SoT framework surfaces new research questions about how LLMs encode and use state through tokens.
future_direction: How do LLMs decide what information to externalize at each cycle?
What information is actually encoded in the state at different points in the sequence?
Do they use consistent encodings across the solution of a problem and across different problems?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate reasoning tokens before their final answer to boost performance on complex tasks. While these sequences seem like human thought processes, empirical evidence reveals that they are not a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state -- the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. This explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We argue that to truly understand the process that LLMs do, research must move beyond reading the reasoning tokens as text and focus on decoding them as state.

papers.title: Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin
papers.research_question: What is the connection between attention sinks and compression valleys in LLMs, and are they driven by a common mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that attention sinks and compression valleys are two manifestations of massive activations in the residual stream, and proposes the Mix-Compress-Refine theory to explain how LLMs organize computation across depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention sinks and compression valleys are unified by massive activations, and the Mix-Compress-Refine framework explains how LLMs allocate computation across depth, with implications for task-dependent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks and compression valleys emerge simultaneously when BOS tokens develop massive activations in middle layers.
Massive activations mathematically induce compression, as proven by Theorem 1 which bounds entropy reduction.
Ablating massive activations (e.g., by zeroing MLP contributions) eliminates both compression and attention sinks, confirming causality.
LLMs process information in three distinct phases: early mixing, middle compression with halted mixing, and late refinement.
Embedding tasks peak during the compression phase, while generation tasks require full refinement through all phases.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focuses on decoder-only transformers; encoder-decoder architectures may exhibit different dynamics.
While models up to 120B parameters are studied, even larger models might show further scaling effects.
Theoretical bounds assume a single massive activation; scenarios with multiple large-norm tokens require extended analysis.
The Mix-Compress-Refine theory needs further validation on a wider range of tasks and architectures.
future_direction: Extend analysis to encoder-decoder architectures.
Investigate the role of positional encodings in phase transitions.
Explore how training objectives shape the emergence of massive activations.
papers.abstract: Attention sinks and compression valleys have attracted significant attention as two puzzling phenomena in large language models, but have been studied in isolation. In this work, we present a surprising connection between attention sinks and compression valleys, tracing both to the formation of massive activations in the residual stream. We prove theoretically that massive activations necessarily produce representational compression and establish bounds on the resulting entropy reduction. Through experiments across several models (410M-120B parameters), we confirm that when the beginning-of-sequence token develops extreme activation norms in the middle layers, both compression valleys and attention sinks emerge simultaneously. Targeted ablation studies validate our theoretical predictions. This unified view motivates us to propose the Mix-Compress-Refine theory of information flow, as an attempt to explain how LLMs organize their computation in depth by controlling attention and representational compression via massive activations. Specifically, we posit that Transformer-based LLMs process tokens in three distinct phases: (1) broad mixing in the early layers, (2) compressed computation with limited mixing in the middle layers, and (3) selective refinement in the late layers. Our framework helps explain why embedding tasks perform best at intermediate layers, whereas generation tasks benefit from full-depth processing, clarifying differences in task-dependent representations.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of research on attention heads in large language models, introducing a novel four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) to categorize attention head functions and summarizing experimental methods for discovering such heads.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on attention heads in LLMs, providing a framework for understanding their functions and the methods used to discover them, while highlighting the need for further work on complex tasks, unified frameworks, alignment with human cognition, generalizability, multi-collaboration, and theoretical support.
papers.key_findings:
The paper proposes a four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) inspired by human thought to categorize the functions of attention heads in LLMs.
It provides a detailed taxonomy of special attention heads, categorizing them by their roles in the four stages and the LLM architectures where they were discovered.
The survey summarizes experimental methodologies for discovering attention heads into two main categories: Modeling-Free (Modification-Based and Replacement-Based) and Modeling-Required (Training-Required and Training-Free).
It describes how attention heads collaborate across different stages to solve complex tasks, using the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task as an example.
The paper outlines current limitations in the field, such as a focus on simple tasks and lack of unified frameworks, and proposes future research directions.
papers.limitation:
Current research primarily focuses on simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning tasks underexplored.
There is a lack of unified frameworks to comprehensively describe the mechanisms of attention heads.
Aligning LLM mechanisms with human cognitive processes remains a significant challenge.
future_direction: Extending research to more complex tasks and real-world applications.
Developing unified frameworks to comprehensively describe attention head mechanisms.
Enhancing alignment between LLM mechanisms and human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, Large Language Models (LLMs) have excelled in various tasks but remain as black-box systems. Understanding the reasoning bottlenecks of LLMs has become a critical challenge, as these limitations are deeply tied to their internal architecture. Among these, attention heads have emerged as a focal point for investigating the underlying mechanics of LLMs. In this survey, we aim to demystify the internal reasoning processes of LLMs by systematically exploring the roles and mechanisms of attention heads. We first introduce a novel four-stage framework inspired by the human thought process: Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, and Expression Preparation. Using this framework, we comprehensively review existing research to identify and categorize the functions of specific attention heads. Additionally, we analyze the experimental methodologies used to discover these special heads, dividing them into two categories: Modeling-Free and Modeling-Required methods. We further summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current research and propose several potential future directions.

papers.title: Llama See, Llama Do: A Mechanistic Perspective on Contextual Entrainment and Distraction in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do language models become distracted by irrelevant contextual information, and what is the mechanistic basis for this distraction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies contextual entrainment, a novel phenomenon where LMs assign higher probabilities to tokens that appear in the context, and discovers entrainment heads that control this effect, providing a mechanistic perspective on distraction.
papers.conclusion: Contextual entrainment is a novel mechanistic phenomenon that plays a crucial role in LM distraction, and interpretability techniques can provide insights for real-world applications such as RAG.
papers.key_findings:
LMs assign significantly higher logits/probabilities to tokens that have appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens (contextual entrainment).
The magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors, with counterfactual prompts having a stronger effect than factual ones.
A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) are responsible for contextual entrainment; disabling them attenuates the effect.
Entrainment heads are relation-specific, not model-specific.
Removing entrainment heads has minimal impact on other LM capabilities like factual recall and in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
Did not conduct experiments using larger LMs due to resource limitations.
Only used the LRE dataset and not standard RAG datasets.
Do not propose an application to mitigate the distraction problem.
future_direction: Reproduce results using larger models.
Validate findings using standard RAG datasets.
Further steps toward addressing the distraction problem.
papers.abstract: We observe a novel phenomenon, contextual entrainment, across a wide range of language models (LMs) and prompt settings, providing a new mechanistic perspective on how LMs become distracted by ``irrelevant'' contextual information in the input prompt. Specifically, LMs assign significantly higher logits (or probabilities) to any tokens that have previously appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens. This suggests that contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, occurring independently of the relevance or semantic relation of the tokens to the question or the rest of the sentence. We find statistically significant evidence that the magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors. Counterfactual prompts have a greater effect compared to factual ones, suggesting that while contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, it is modulated by semantic factors. We hypothesise that there is a circuit of attention heads -- the entrainment heads -- that corresponds to the contextual entrainment phenomenon. Using a novel entrainment head discovery method based on differentiable masking, we identify these heads across various settings. When we ``turn off'' these heads, i.e., set their outputs to zero, the effect of contextual entrainment is significantly attenuated, causing the model to generate output that capitulates to what it would produce if no distracting context were provided. Our discovery of contextual entrainment, along with our investigation into LM distraction via the entrainment heads, marks a key step towards the mechanistic analysis and mitigation of the distraction problem.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
papers.research_question: Do latent tokens in Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT) actually encode reasoning, or do they merely simulate the appearance of it?
papers.core_contribution: Latent tokens in COCONUT function as uninterpretable placeholders and promote shortcut usage, rather than encoding faithful reasoning, leading to inflated benchmark performance without true reasoning.
papers.conclusion: COCONUT tokens serve as pseudo-reasoning placeholders, are not semantically interpretable, and exhibit shortcut behaviors, indicating that latent reasoning in COCONUT is not faithful.
papers.key_findings:
COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering perturbations (PSR <5%) compared to CoT tokens (PSR up to 50%), indicating they lack reasoning-critical information.
Token-swapping experiments show COCONUT's accuracy remains stable after swapping, while CoT's drops, indicating latent tokens have limited influence on final predictions.
COCONUT exhibits strong shortcut dependence, e.g., in MMLU with biased options, incorrect predictions selecting the biased option rise to 70%.
In HotpotQA, COCONUT shows extreme sensitivity to shortcut manipulation, with accuracy dropping to near 0% when shortcuts favor incorrect answers.
PCA visualizations show latent token embeddings are distributed far from the main vocabulary manifold, indicating they act as placeholders without semantic meaning.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not establish a formal causal link between latent representations and reasoning quality.
The study did not deeply investigate the reasons why COCONUT relies on shortcuts, so the analysis remains speculative.
future_direction: Investigate more challenging out-of-distribution evaluations.
Design reasoning-specialized LLM baselines.
Develop novel interpretability metrics to probe latent reasoning traces.
papers.abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
